name: Cryptic crossword No 22,611
preamble: Many solutions refer to products of West London.

clue.text: In a theatrical company of aesthetes mine host is an elephant

definitions.note: the party is known by its elephant emblem

indicators.note: the landlord sits inside the stage company, as if standing in it

blocks.note: a rep is a repertory theatre company
'mine host' is the old jocular name for an innkeeper
aesthetes are arty types

explanation.surface: A pub landlord turns up as the elephant in an arty amateur theatre show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' acts only on the theatre company, not on the arty word that follows. 'Mine host' is an old-fashioned jocular term for a pub landlord.
explanation.definitionFit: The American Republicans have used an elephant as their emblem since a nineteenth-century cartoon by Thomas Nast.

clue.text: Girl's garment in boy, or peninsula (with 18?)

indicators.note: the item of clothing is placed inside the word for a youngster

blocks.note: a lad is a boy
an undergarment worn by women
taken as written

explanation.surface: A girl's bra turns up with a boy, or so it seems.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracketed hint points to 18-down: a Labrador is also a dog breed, whose hairs get everywhere.
explanation.definitionFit: Labrador is the large Canadian landmass jutting between Hudson Bay and the Atlantic, a peninsula.

clue.text: See 17
Postprandial request as entry to Pimlico?

blocks.note: first meaning: after dinner one asks the table to send the decanter round
second meaning: the document admitting you to a place

explanation.walkthrough: Read as two words it is the after-dinner 'pass the port'. Pimlico is a district of London; the 1949 Ealing film imagines it declaring itself part of Burgundy.
explanation.definitionFit: A travel document grants admission to a country, so it is literally one's entry; the film title supplies Pimlico.

clue.text: Suit of a kind?

blocks.note: first meaning: one of the four sets in a pack of cards
second meaning: the word that follows Kind in the Ealing film Kind ... and Coronets

explanation.walkthrough: 'Of a kind' looks like 'of a certain type', but it means the word that goes with Kind in the 1949 Ealing film title.
explanation.definitionFit: Hearts is one of the four card suits, and it follows Kind in the film Kind Hearts and Coronets.

clue.text: Umpire disoriented top people in the USSR

indicators.note: the word does two jobs: split up, its tail oriented means arranged anew, acting on the letters before it

blocks.note: taken as written
the first three letters of the clue's last word, taken as written

explanation.surface: A referee has lost his bearings on the field.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Disoriented' looks like one anagram word acting on Umpire alone, but Umpire has only six letters; split it as dis + oriented.
explanation.definitionFit: The Presidium was the standing executive committee of the Soviet state, so its members were the country's top people.

clue.text: See 13
Hold ball? Never! I'm dispersing these so-called musicians

indicators.note: dispersing scatters these letters so they can regroup in a new order

blocks.note: all the letters of these words are used

explanation.surface: Someone at a game refuses to keep hold of the ball and breaks up a crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: The 1951 Ealing comedy The Lavender Hill Mob is about a gang of bullion robbers; Lavender Hill is a street in south London.
explanation.definitionFit: A band of musicians and a mob of crooks are both groups, so the gang is jokily 'so-called musicians'.

clue.text: The Spanish sailor's nil charge is complex

blocks.note: el is Spanish for 'the'
AB, able-bodied seaman, is a sailor
the figure zero
a rate is a charge or fee

explanation.surface: A Spanish seaman's zero-fee arrangement turns out to be complicated.
explanation.definitionFit: Something elaborate is intricate and detailed, made up of many interconnected parts.

clue.text: The Sun is a female in Russia

blocks.note: Ra was the Egyptian sun god
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A tabloid headline claims a Russian woman.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sun looks like the British tabloid; it is the god Ra.
explanation.definitionFit: Raisa is a common Russian woman's first name, borne by Raisa Gorbachev, wife of the last Soviet leader.

clue.text: Increases the amount of upper-class chatters

blocks.note: U is the old label for upper-class usage
to prate is to chatter

explanation.surface: Posh people's gossip only grows.
explanation.definitionFit: To uprate a payment or pension is to raise its level, as when benefits are adjusted for inflation.

clue.text: Will you do this again?

blocks.note: first meaning: determination, a noun
second meaning: read as ..., what a solver would do on a second attempt at the puzzle

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as a question to the solver; 'Will' is a noun, and the second part is the answer split as re-solve.
explanation.definitionFit: Resolve and will both mean firm determination to carry something through.

clue.text: Lard likely to cook one of the hunks?

indicators.note: to cook something is to work it into a new form, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: all the letters of the two words

explanation.surface: Fat is going to be cooked by one of the beefy men.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ladykillers (1955) is the Ealing comedy about a gang lodging with an old woman.
explanation.definitionFit: A handsome charmer who wins many women's hearts is a ladykiller, much as a hunk is.

clue.text: Thought to be legally placed in the estimation of the street?

indicators.note: the legal position is put inside the reputation term

blocks.note: street cred is standing among one's peers
in football a player onside is in a lawful position

explanation.surface: Something is judged lawful in the eyes of ordinary people.
explanation.walkthrough: Onside is the football term for a player in a legal position; cred is short for credibility, as in 'street cred'.
explanation.definitionFit: Considered as an adjective means regarded or judged, the past participle sense of thought.

clue.text: Nameless feeler with endless story taking place during confinement

indicators.note: 'less' attached to Name asks for the abbreviation of name to be dropped
without an end, so the final letter is cut off

blocks.note: an insect's feeler
a tale is a story

explanation.surface: An insect's feeler, missing a name, goes with a story that never ends.
explanation.walkthrough: One N (name) goes from ANTENNA and the E from TALE.
explanation.definitionFit: Confinement is the old term for pregnancy and childbirth, so prenatal care happens during it.

clue.text: Love in an old officer, one of those associated with 5

indicators.note: the zero is placed inside the military rank

blocks.note: a cornet was the lowest commissioned cavalry officer
love is zero in tennis, shaped like O

explanation.surface: A romance blossoms with a retired army officer.
explanation.walkthrough: 5 is HEARTS: the Ealing film is Kind Hearts and Coronets.
explanation.definitionFit: Coronets are the small crowns of the peers Alec Guinness plays in Kind Hearts and Coronets, so they are paired with hearts.

clue.text: One of these surprises was associated with 17 down

definitions.note: the singular film title, fair because 'one of these' names a single member of the plural

blocks.note: first meaning: sudden shocks out of the blue
second meaning: a single such bolt gives the film title linked to the village at 17-down

explanation.walkthrough: 17-down is TITFIELD: The Titfield Thunderbolt (1953) is the Ealing comedy about villagers saving their branch railway and its old engine.
explanation.definitionFit: A sudden shocking piece of news is a bolt from the blue, so the plural noun means shocks.

clue.text: Bird on meadow was on line

definitions.note: the place where the film's branch railway ran

blocks.note: a small songbird
a meadow is a field

explanation.surface: A small bird settles on a grassy field and then on a wire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On line' looks like modern internet talk; it means the railway line serving the fictional village in The Titfield Thunderbolt.
explanation.definitionFit: Titfield is the invented village whose railway branch the Ealing film's locals fight to keep running.

clue.text: Souvenirs of friend Diana, who keeps one in butter

blocks.note: surface reading: keepsakes from a friend called Diana
setter's reading: the friend is a pet, and Diana's pet leaves its traces even in the butter dish

explanation.walkthrough: A dog is man's best friend; the stray reminders it leaves around the house turn up even in the butter. 2-down's Labrador points the same way.
explanation.definitionFit: Shed fur is what a pet leaves behind, so it serves as an unwelcome keepsake of the animal.

clue.text: Further levels reached when changing numbers

indicators.note: changing the word means swapping its letters round

blocks.note: taken as written
eights are numbers

explanation.surface: Higher levels are attained by altering the figures.
explanation.walkthrough: 'When' looks like a link word, but it is the anagram fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: To reach new heights is the idiom for attaining a higher level of success than ever before.

clue.text: Beater, in the past a young lady with plenty of spirit

indicators.note: the young woman is placed inside the expression for long ago

blocks.note: a whisk is a kitchen beater
days of yore are the past
gal is informal for a girl

explanation.surface: A wife-beater from long ago was once a spirited young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: Whisky Galore! (1949) is the Ealing comedy about islanders salvaging whisky from a wrecked ship.
explanation.definitionFit: Galore means in abundance, so whisky galore is the phrase for spirits in plentiful supply.

clue.text: See 20
Fruit taken from William in Italy

indicators.note: the answer is what remains when outer letters are taken away from the translated name

blocks.note: the Italian form of the name William

explanation.surface: Someone brings fruit back from a man named William in Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters are not in the clue: translate William into Italian, then drop the G at the front and the ELMO at the back.
explanation.definitionFit: The ugli is a Jamaican citrus fruit, a cross of grapefruit and tangerine with knobbly skin.

clue.text: Colour of the man's suit, a success in the Guardian

indicators.note: the success sits inside the newspaper's word for itself

blocks.note: a newspaper's editorial voice speaks of itself as 'we'
a hit is a success

explanation.surface: The colour of a man's outfit is a smash hit in a newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: The Man in the White Suit (1951) is the Ealing comedy about an indestructible fabric.
explanation.definitionFit: The film's inventor wears a suit of his gleaming new cloth, so the suit's colour is the title's.

clue.text: A giant to be sick for a maid

blocks.note: taken as written
giant means big
to ail is to be ill

explanation.surface: A giant is due to fall ill and needs a servant.
explanation.definitionFit: Abigail is an old literary term for a lady's maid, from a waiting-woman in a seventeenth-century play.

clue.text: Antisocial person hails me, strangely

indicators.note: the letters behave strangely, coming out in an unexpected order

blocks.note: all the letters of the two words

explanation.surface: An unsociable type greets the speaker oddly.
explanation.definitionFit: Ishmael, cast out in Genesis, became the byword for an outcast set against society.

clue.text: One of 5, say, in Indian

definitions.note: an Indian dish, adjective standing for a noun

indicators.note: say asks us to voice the word and spell what we hear differently

blocks.note: 5 is the plural of a word for the organ in your chest; ticker is slang for it

explanation.surface: One of a set of cards, in an Indian setting.
explanation.walkthrough: 5-down is HEARTS; a heart is a ticker in slang, and in a non-rhotic accent that is pronounced like the curry dish.
explanation.definitionFit: Tikka is a South Asian dish of marinated chunks of meat cooked on skewers, so it is Indian food.

clue.text: The Conqueror's ancestor entertains some Tories: "I'd love to _____ some day before I'm old" (Kipling)

definitions.text: I'd love to _____ some day before I'm old

indicators.note: only part of the party members' word is wanted, the tail being dropped
to entertain is to hold a guest within, so one name goes around the other

blocks.note: the Viking founder of Normandy, forebear of William the Conqueror
members of the Conservative Party

explanation.surface: William the Conqueror's forebear plays host to a few Conservatives, then a line of Kipling.
explanation.walkthrough: Rollo was the Viking who founded the Duchy of Normandy. The quotation is from Kipling's Just So Verses.
explanation.definitionFit: Kipling's poem Roll Down to Rio has the speaker longing to travel to Rio de Janeiro someday, which fills the gap.
